summary.text: The proof uses the same factorial obstruction twice: for \(m\ge4\) and \(2\le k\le m\), the number \(m!-k\) is composite because \(k\mid m!\) and \(k\) is a proper divisor of \(m!-k\). Assuming either relevant prime family is bounded by \(N\), apply the decomposition hypothesis to \((N+2)!/6=x+y\); boundedness makes respectively \(6x-1\) or \(6y+1\) an admissible \(k\), forcing the complementary required prime \(6y+1\) or \(6x-1\) to be composite, a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\mathcal S=\{p\in\mathbb N: p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
\mathcal T=\{r\in\mathbb N:r\text{ is prime and }r+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of lower members of twin-prime pairs. Since a twin-prime pair is uniquely determined by its lower member, infinitude of \(\mathcal T\) is exactly infinitude of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(a(n)=A227923(n)\) counts the integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\) for which, on putting \(y=n-x\), all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are prime. Thus \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime, because
\[
2(6x-1)+1=12x-1,
\]
and \(6y-1,6y+1\) are a twin-prime pair. We assume throughout that
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.
\]
We prove that both \(\mathcal S\) and \(\mathcal T\) are infinite.

First observe explicitly what positivity of \(a(n)\) gives. Its defining sum is a finite sum indexed by \(1\le x<n\), and every summand is either \(0\) or \(1\), according as the four primality conditions above fail or hold. If the sum is positive, at least one summand is \(1\). Consequently, whenever \(n>1\), there is an integer \(x\) satisfying \(1\le x<n\) such that, with \(y=n-x\),
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\]
are all prime. Since \(x<n\), we have \(y>0\), and \(n=x+y\). In particular,
\[
6n=6x+6y=(6x-1)+(6y+1). \tag{1}
\]

We will use the following elementary factorial fact.

**Factorial obstruction.** If \(M\ge4\) and \(2\le k\le M\), then \(M!-k\) is not prime.

Indeed, because \(1\le k\le M\), the integer \(k\) divides \(M!\), and hence it also divides \(M!-k\). Moreover,
\[
2k\le2M<M!.
\]
To justify the strict inequality, write
\[
M!=M(M-1)!.
\]
Since \(M\ge4\), we have \((M-1)!\ge3!=6>2\), so multiplication by the positive integer \(M\) gives \(2M<M!\). It follows from \(2k<M!\) that
\[
k<M!-k.
\]
Thus \(M!-k\) has a divisor \(k\) with
\[
1<k<M!-k,
\]
so it cannot be prime. This proves the factorial obstruction.

We now prove the two required infinitude statements separately.

### Infinitely many Sophie Germain primes

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(\mathcal S\) is finite. A finite set of natural numbers is bounded, so there is an integer \(N\ge4\) such that
\[
p\le N\qquad\text{for every }p\in\mathcal S. \tag{2}
\]
Set
\[
M=N+2,
\qquad
n=\frac{M!}{6}.
\]
Here \(M=N+2\ge6\), so \(6\mid M!\), and therefore \(n\) is an integer satisfying
\[
6n=M!. \tag{3}
\]
Also \(M!\ge6!=720\), whence
\[
n=\frac{M!}{6}\ge120>1.
\]
The hypothesis \(a(n)>0\) therefore supplies positive integers \(x,y\) with \(n=x+y\) such that
\[
p:=6x-1,

a:=12x-1,

r:=6y-1,

q:=6y+1
\]
are all prime.

The first two primality conditions show that \(p\) is a Sophie Germain prime: since \(x>0\), ordinary integer arithmetic gives
\[
2p+1=2(6x-1)+1=12x-1=a,
\]
which is prime. Thus \(p\in\mathcal S\), and the assumed bound (2) yields
\[
p\le N<M=N+2. \tag{4}
\]
As \(p\) is prime, \(p\ge2\). Hence
\[
2\le p\le M.
\]

On the other hand, equations (1) and (3) give
\[
M!=6n=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=p+q.
\]
Therefore
\[
q=M!-p. \tag{5}
\]
The factorial obstruction, applied with \(k=p\), says that \(M!-p\) is not prime, because \(M\ge4\) and \(2\le p\le M\). By (5), this says that \(q=6y+1\) is not prime. But \(q\) was one of the four primes supplied by the decomposition counted by \(a(n)\). This contradiction shows that \(\mathcal S\) cannot be finite. Therefore there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes.

### Infinitely many twin-prime pairs

Suppose instead, for contradiction, that \(\mathcal T\) is finite. Again choose an integer \(N\ge4\) bounding all its elements:
\[
r\le N\qquad\text{for every }r\in\mathcal T. \tag{6}
\]
As before, put
\[
M=N+2,

gap
n=\frac{M!}{6}.
\]
Once again \(M\ge6\), so \(n\) is an integer, \(n>1\), and
\[
6n=M!. \tag{7}
\]
By the assumption \(a(n)>0\), choose \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\), put \(y=n-x>0\), and obtain primality of
\[
p:=6x-1,

12x-1,

r:=6y-1,

q:=6y+1.
\]
Since \(y>0\),
\[
r+2=(6y-1)+2=6y+1=q.
\]
Thus \(r\) and \(r+2=q\) are both prime, so \(r\in\mathcal T\). The bound (6) gives
\[
r\le N.
\]
Consequently,
\[
q=r+2\le N+2=M. \tag{8}
\]
Also \(q\ge2\); indeed, it is prime (and even directly \(y\ge1\) gives \(q=6y+1\ge7\)). Hence
\[
2\le q\le M.
\]

Using the decomposition identity (1) together with (7), we now have
\[
M!=6n=(6x-1)+(6y+1)=p+q,
\]
and therefore
\[
p=M!-q. \tag{9}
\]
Apply the factorial obstruction with \(k=q\). The inequalities just obtained imply that \(M!-q\) is not prime. By (9), this means that \(p=6x-1\) is not prime, contradicting the primality of \(6x-1\) furnished by the decomposition counted by \(a(n)\). Therefore \(\mathcal T\) is infinite.

We have proved both that the set of Sophie Germain primes is infinite and that the set of lower members of twin-prime pairs is infinite. Equivalently, there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and infinitely many twin-prime pairs.
